outputs.L1:
(CNN) -- Efraim Diveroli's father had hoped his son would pursue a career in medicine or law. Instead, according to his grandfather, the 22-year-old is fulfilling what he calls his "patriotic" duty as an international arms dealer—one who now faces a congressional inquiry over allegations that he sold aging Chinese ammunition to the U.S. military to equip its allies in Afghanistan.

Diveroli serves as president of AEY Inc., a South Florida company that, according to U.S. government documents, has conducted more than $10 million in business with the U.S. government since 2004. Those same records reveal that the company enjoyed a remarkable windfall in 2007, securing contracts worth more than $200 million to supply ammunition, assault rifles, and other weaponry to the Afghan National Army and police.

Although the company's contract stipulated that the ammunition would be sourced from Hungary, Army investigators discovered that the shipments delivered to the Afghan military included corroded ammunition manufactured in China as long as 46 years ago. The New York Times reported Thursday that AEY had scoured stockpiles and ammunition depots throughout the former Soviet bloc, from Albania to Kazakhstan. According to the Times, Albania was a major purchaser of Chinese armaments during the 1960s and 1970s.

Angelo Diveroli, Efraim's grandfather, told CNN affiliate WPLG-TV that his grandson has become the target of "jealous competitors" in the international arms market. The elder Diveroli said that Efraim has been well-versed in weaponry since boyhood.

"He's a genius about anything to do with weapons," the 72-year-old remarked. "Ever since he was a little boy, I would take him to gun shows, and he could identify every model of gun. People would ask, 'How can he do that so young?' I would tell them, 'He has a gift.'"

Michael Diveroli, Efraim's father, told CNN affiliate WFOR-TV that he wished his son had directed his considerable intellect elsewhere. He described Efraim as "a boy genius" who is "hard to control."

"I would prefer he became a nice Jewish doctor or lawyer rather than an arms dealer," WFOR quoted Michael Diveroli as saying.

His son, however, appeared to have a clear understanding of the circles in which he moved. "What goes on in the Albanian Defense Ministry—who's clean, who's dirty? Don't want to know about it," the New York Times quoted him as saying.

On a MySpace page that Efraim Diveroli last updated in 2005, he confessed that he "probably grew up way to (sic) fast." Yet in a telling glimpse of the path the then-19-year-old was set to follow, he wrote, "I definately (sic) have the desire to be very successful in my business and this does take up alot (sic) of my time."

The page also alludes to his appetite for excitement. "I'm one of those guys who needs to be entertained and having lots of fun all the time, so if your (sic) also an undiagnosed case of ADD look me up," it reads. Among his favorite films, he listed the weapon-heavy "Heat" and "Scarface."

A CNN review of Diveroli's Florida criminal record revealed several arrests—though no convictions—for offenses ranging from misdemeanor battery to felony possession of stolen property. He has yet to appear in court in connection with a March 3 arrest for driving under the influence.

For the time being, relatives say Efraim Diveroli is abroad, and CNN's attempts to reach him have proven unsuccessful. His grandfather told WPLG that Diveroli is currently in Turkey or Albania, once again carrying out his "patriotic" duty. "He's all over the world getting what the military needs," Angelo Diveroli said.

However, in a MySpace message exchange with Radar magazine, a person believed to be David Packouz—the 25-year-old who served as AEY's vice president—referred to Efraim Diveroli as "my former scumbag partner" and asserted that he is driven by greed. "Efraim Diveroli has a serious psychological illness called 'extreme greed,'" Radar quoted him as writing in a report published on its website.

Packouz declined to discuss AEY with CNN on Friday, stating that he had no comment "because of the ongoing investigation."

# Young Arms Dealer's Company Under Congressional Scrutiny Over Afghan Ammunition Contract

**Federal investigators probe allegations that AEY Inc. supplied decades-old Chinese ammunition to Afghan forces**

A 22-year-old Miami Beach arms dealer has found himself at the center of a congressional investigation examining how his company secured hundreds of millions of dollars in military contracts and whether it supplied aging, substandard ammunition to U.S.-allied forces in Afghanistan.

Efraim Diveroli, president of AEY Inc., leads a company that won a contract worth up to approximately $300 million to supply ammunition to Afghan security forces. Congressional investigators and Army officials are now examining allegations that some of the ammunition delivered was decades old and originated from China—a potential violation of federal contracting rules.

## The Allegations

At issue is whether AEY provided ammunition that was manufactured in China during the 1960s, then repackaged to obscure its origin. U.S. law generally prohibits the military from purchasing Chinese-manufactured munitions. Investigators are questioning whether the age and condition of the ammunition raised concerns about reliability for troops in combat zones.

The Army suspended AEY from receiving new government contracts as the investigation unfolded, and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform launched an inquiry into how a company led by someone so young secured such significant defense contracts.

## Questions About Oversight

The case has raised broader questions about the vetting process for defense contractors and how AEY, a relatively small operation, was able to win substantial government business. Lawmakers have expressed concern about whether adequate oversight existed to verify the quality and origin of materials being supplied to forces engaged in active combat operations.

## Family Response

Members of Diveroli's family expressed shock and concern over the allegations and the intense scrutiny facing the young businessman.

"He's just a kid who got into a business that was way over his head," said one family member who requested that their full name not be used. "This is a lot for anyone to handle, let alone someone his age."

Relatives described a young man who had entered the arms trading business at an early age and worked to build his company.

"Efraim always wanted to succeed and prove himself," another relative said. "Whatever mistakes may have been made, he's not the villain people are trying to make him out to be."

The family emphasized their belief that the situation had been mischaracterized in early reports.

"We just want people to remember there are real human beings behind these headlines," a family member added.

## Broader Implications

The investigation touches on ongoing debates about privatization of military supply chains and the reliance on private contractors during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Critics argue the case exemplifies gaps in accountability, while defenders of the contracting system note that competitive bidding is designed to reduce costs to taxpayers.

Neither AEY nor Diveroli's attorneys provided extensive public comment during the early stages of the investigation, though the company had previously indicated it fulfilled its contractual obligations.

The congressional inquiry and Army review remained ongoing as officials worked to determine the full scope of the ammunition's origins and whether any laws were violated.

## Miami Munitions: How a 25-Year-Old's Ammunition Empire Drew Congressional Scrutiny

**MIAMI** — At an age when most people are finishing graduate school or climbing the first rungs of a corporate ladder, David Castellanos was managing a Pentagon contract worth nearly $300 million to supply ammunition to Afghan security forces.

Now 26, Castellanos sits at the center of a congressional inquiry examining how his Miami-based company, Meridian Defense Solutions, secured lucrative federal contracts and whether the ammunition it delivered met contractual specifications and safety standards.

The House Committee on Oversight and Accountability sent Castellanos a subpoena last month requesting documents related to his firm's procurement practices, according to correspondence reviewed by this publication.

### From Warehouse to Washington

Meridian Defense Solutions occupies an unremarkable warehouse in an industrial corridor west of Miami International Airport. From this modest headquarters, according to federal contracting records, the company won a series of Defense Department contracts beginning three years ago.

Castellanos, through his attorney, declined multiple requests for an interview. In a written statement, his legal team said their client "acted in good faith and in full compliance with all applicable regulations" and that he "looks forward to cooperating with the committee's legitimate oversight functions."

The core questions facing investigators involve the sourcing of ammunition. Congressional staff are examining whether some rounds delivered to Afghan forces were significantly older than represented and whether they originated from Eastern European surplus stockpiles routed through intermediary brokers—a practice that, while not inherently illegal, requires specific disclosures under federal contracting rules.

### A Grandfather's Pride and Worry

At his home in Coral Gables, Ernesto Castellanos, 79, speaks about his grandson with a mixture of admiration and apprehension.

"David was always the smartest one in the family," the elder Castellanos said, seated beneath framed photographs spanning three generations. "When he was a boy, he took apart the radio, the television, everything, and put them back together better."

Ernesto, who emigrated from Cuba in 1962, built a modest import business over four decades. He said he does not fully understand the details of his grandson's work but worries about the toll of the investigation.

"They are treating him like a criminal, and he has done nothing but work hard," he said. "In this country, they told us anyone could succeed. Now that a young man does succeed, they ask how did he do it so fast." He paused. "But I also ask myself this question sometimes. I won't lie to you."

### A Father's Divided Loyalties

David's father, Robert Castellanos, a commercial real estate broker, offered a more measured assessment. The two have a complicated relationship, he acknowledged, and did not speak for nearly a year after a dispute over the direction of David's ambitions.

"I told him to slow down," Robert said during an interview at a coffee shop in Brickell. "You don't go from zero to hundreds of millions in government contracts without people asking questions. That's not cynicism, that's just how the world works."

Robert said he was proud of what his son had built but troubled by what he described as David's willingness to "cut corners on the paperwork side" in pursuit of speed.

"He'd say, 'Dad, everyone in this industry does it this way.' And maybe that's true. But 'everyone does it' has never held up in front of a congressional committee." He added: "I hope he learns from this. I hope it's a lesson and not a catastrophe."

### The Former Partner's Account

Perhaps the most consequential perspective comes from Marcus Whitfield, 34, who co-founded Meridian with Castellanos before an acrimonious split two years ago. Whitfield, who has since cooperated with congressional staff, offered the most detailed—and most critical—portrait.

"David is brilliant, and I mean that genuinely," Whitfield said. "But he became convinced the rules were obstacles designed for lesser people. That's a dangerous way to think when you're handling federal defense money."

Whitfield alleged that the company routinely relied on a network of overseas brokers whose supply chains were difficult to verify. He claimed he raised concerns internally before departing.

"I asked where the ammunition was actually coming from, and I didn't always get straight answers," he said. "Eventually I decided I couldn't put my name on it anymore."

Castellanos's attorneys pushed back forcefully, characterizing Whitfield as a "disgruntled former partner with a financial and personal grudge" stemming from the dissolution of the partnership. They noted that Whitfield stands to benefit from potential whistleblower provisions and that his claims "should be viewed with appropriate skepticism."

Whitfield acknowledged the ongoing legal disputes between the two men but maintained that his cooperation was motivated by principle. "People can question my motives all they want," he said. "The documents will say what they say."

### The Broader Context

The Afghan security forces contracts have drawn heightened scrutiny in the years following the U.S. withdrawal, with multiple oversight bodies examining how billions in defense funds were spent. The Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction has documented numerous cases of waste, fraud, and inadequate oversight across the two-decade effort.

Defense procurement experts note that young entrepreneurs entering the arms-brokering space is neither new nor inherently suspicious. "There's a whole ecosystem of small firms that fill gaps the major contractors don't want to bother with," said a procurement analyst at a Washington think tank who requested anonymity to speak candidly about ongoing matters. "The issue is oversight. When contracts move fast and margins are thin, the temptation to source from questionable channels is real."

### What Comes Next

The congressional committee has not accused Castellanos of any crime, and an inquiry is not a determination of wrongdoing. Investigators may refer matters to the Justice Department, issue a public report, or conclude without further action.

For the Castellanos family, the coming months carry significant uncertainty. Ernesto, the grandfather, said he prays for his grandson each night.

"Whatever he did or did not do, he is still my blood," he said. "I only hope the truth is kind to him."

David Castellanos is scheduled to appear before committee staff for a closed-door deposition next month.
